title: Physiological determinants of ultramarathon trail-running performance
authors: Coates AM, Berard JA, King TJ, Burr JF
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
population: Athletes finishing a 50-, 80- or 160-km trail race on a 20-km loop course on the same day; performance defined as percent difference from the winning time
findings: In the 50-km race, training volumes, cardiovascular health, aerobic fitness and a greater loss of body mass were related to better performance (all P < .05).

Peak velocity in the VO2max test was the best predictor in the 50-km race (men: beta = -11.7, P = .002, with baseline blood pressure, r2 = .96; women: beta = -13.6, P = .001, with body-mass loss, r2 = .87).
In the 80-km race only peak velocity from the VO2max test predicted performance (beta = -20.3, r2 = .78, P < .001).
In the 160-km race there were no significant performance determinants; the authors conclude performance in longer races appears less influenced by such physiological parameters.
limitations: Group sizes not stated in the abstract; very high r2 values suggest overfitting with small samples; the 160-km null result may reflect low power and finisher-only samples.
implications: Keep VO2max-test peak velocity (or a field equivalent such as recent 5 or 10 km speed) as a performance predictor for 50 to 80 km goals only.
For 100-mile goal-time estimates, widen the prediction interval and rely less on speed-based fitness; do not present a precise time from fitness alone.
Treat the 160-km null result as a reason for finish-first plan framing, not as evidence that fitness is irrelevant.

verification.notes: Crossref (2021-10-01) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched; all numbers confirmed.
